name: Inuit diet

lead: The traditional Inuit diet is built on seal, walrus, whale, caribou, fish, birds and some gathered plants, often eaten raw, frozen or boiled. In diet communities it is cited as a high-protein, high-fat, low-carbohydrate pattern that supports leanness and muscle.

Researchers describe roughly half of calories from fat, 30-35% from protein and 15-20% from carbohydrate, and have studied it for omega-3 intake and heart health. Findings on cardiovascular protection are debated.

paras: People inspired by it emphasise fatty fish, red meat and organ meats, and sometimes raw or lightly cooked preparations; access to marine-mammal foods is limited outside Arctic communities.

Traditional foods can carry environmental contaminants such as methylmercury, and studies report Inuit heart disease rates similar to other populations and higher stroke mortality. Dietary transition to store-bought food is linked to health problems in Arctic communities.

angle.text: Followers use the diet as a template for a meat- and fish-centred, low-carbohydrate pattern. They report that it helps them stay lean while keeping protein high enough to build muscle.

lead: The traditional Inuit diet is an animal-based pattern of hunted, fished and gathered foods, including ringed and bearded seal, walrus, whales, caribou, muskox, birds and eggs, Arctic char and cod, with berries, roots and seaweed.[1] Food is often eaten frozen, raw or boiled with few seasonings; dishes include akutaq, igunaq and suaasat.[1]

People interested in physique and body composition cite it as an example of a high-fat, high-protein, low-carbohydrate way of eating that supported lean, strong bodies; that is a belief of followers rather than a research finding. Traditional diets derived roughly 50% of calories from fat, 30-35% from protein and 15-20% from carbohydrate, much of the latter from glycogen in raw meat, and several studies found the diet was not ketogenic.[1]

Researchers have studied the omega-3 content and heart disease. The 'Inuit paradox' idea held that omega-3-rich fats protected against heart disease, but later work found coronary disease rates similar to non-Inuit populations and about double the North American stroke mortality risk; a 2014 critique found the original Danish studies never established low rates.[1]

paras: Marine mammals central to the diet include ringed and bearded seal, walrus and whales such as narwhal, beluga and bowhead; land animals include caribou, polar bear and muskox.[1] Plants such as berries, grasses, tubers and seaweed are gathered, and akutaq combines berries with fat.[1]

Vitamins A and D come from oils and livers of cold-water fish and mammals, and vitamin C from raw or frozen foods such as muktuk, seal brain, kelp and reindeer liver, which preserves what cooking would destroy.[1] Studies from the 1970s found enlarged livers and high urea output, which the article links to protein used for energy.[1]

A study of Nunavik Inuit examined n-3 fatty acids and cardiovascular risk factors.[2] Research on the gut microbiome reports that the Inuit gut microbiome is dynamic over time and shaped by traditional foods.[3] A scoping review examined drivers and health implications of the dietary transition among Canadian Arctic Inuit.[4]
Fish oil supplement trials have not consistently shown protection against heart attacks or strokes.[1]

Store-bought food has increasingly replaced traditional food, which has been linked to health problems and food insecurity, while costs of snowmobiles, rifles and fuel have reduced hunting by many families.[1][4] A Greenland study examined food reward after a traditional versus westernised diet.[5]

Studies are mostly observational and population-based, including the Nunavik fatty acid study[2] and a Greenland dietary intervention on food reward.[5] No trials have tested adopting an Inuit-style diet for appearance outcomes.
